source_document.body:
Drug developers increasingly have the option of seeking regulatory approval and commercializing a medicine themselves, rather than accepting an early exit offer. Doing so requires a worldwide strategy.
The biotech funding rebound presents a strategic choice for small drug developers that was not available during the post-pandemic slump. Rather than accept an early partnership or acquisition to keep the lights on, many companies now have the funding runway to retain their assets longer and advance them further on their own. But exercising that independence increasingly requires a global regulatory strategy with parallel submissions.
In my position at Parexel, I’ve worked directly with biotech CEOs who recognize that executing this strategy demands a level of regional reach their companies do not have in-house. They’re looking for help in navigating this new regulatory playbook. They understand that seeking approval overseas is not a replacement for the FDA pathway; it’s a parallel and necessary approach. Pursuing approvals in multiple markets simultaneously allows sponsors to de-risk their dependence on any single agency while also accelerating patient access globally.
The FDA is still the regulatory anchor, but others are growing more competitive
The FDA and regulators in other major markets have been making deliberate moves to streamline their processes and attract development activity. The result is a regulatory landscape that looks meaningfully different from the one companies were operating in even a few years ago.
In the U.S., the FDA continues to incentivize high-value, differentiated programs, including through unmet need designations, orphan drug status and personalized medicine. In this environment, the clarity of a submission is key, as a poorly constructed dossier or an insufficiently justified development plan carries greater risk of delay or rejection.
Japan’s Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Agency (PMDA) has opened up to global assets, adding offices in the U.S. in late 2024 to provide consultation and support for overseas companies with no presence in Japan. The U.K. Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) has cleared its backlog and just rolled out new regulations governing the clinical trial application process, with timelines that are now beating the FDA. The European Medicines Agency (EMA) has similarly become more attractive for parallel engagement, launching EU-CTR to support single-application, multi-country trial approvals. The agency has initiated several pilot projects, such as FAST-EU, to accelerate trial authorization.
This competitive global dynamic is reshaping where and how biotechs pursue development. Historically, the path was sequential: secure FDA approval first, then expand to the EMA, and finally to other regions, often much later. Now, parallel submissions are becoming the norm.
These require more than filing to multiple agencies at once. They require parallel regulatory input on your development plan from the start. Multi-regional perspectives must be built into protocol design, not incorporated at the point of filing. Failure to integrate early will almost inevitably lead to inefficiencies, delays or sub-optimal global outcomes—risks that are disproportionately impactful for smaller organizations. For a small company without expertise in every region, this process can be a significant strain.
Execution risk is real
Choosing to advance independently is a significant operational undertaking. Many companies have never navigated Phase 2 and Phase 3 with the FDA on their own. They lack bandwidth across multiple regions and are running trials in an environment where clinical sites are saturated and investigator costs are rising due to inflation.
Given this, flawless operational execution has never mattered more. There is little margin for error when a regulatory agency is operating under capacity constraints and resubmission is costly. A well-designed, derisked submission is no longer just good practice; it is critical risk management.
Biotechs are no longer deliberating between the traditional options of seeking a partner or an acquisition. They must build global development plans from day one with parallel submissions as a core element, not as something they can address once the FDA path is established.
The regulatory landscape has shifted in ways that make the independent path more viable, but only for those who plan and execute with rigor and the right infrastructure. This will ensure parallel submissions are not just feasible, but strategically optimized.

The largest pharmas have a collective $188 billion in firepower to spend on M&A transactions, with all but one signaling a desire to execute, according to a new analysis from Leerink Partners.
Big Pharmas are reaching into their wallets as M&A returns to the sector, with four major companies having the deepest pockets for transactions, according to a recent analysis from Leerink Partners.
Johnson & Johnson leads the pack with $21 billion in cash on hand and is the most likely to buy when market cap and executive commentary are also factored in, according to Leerink’s October 18 report on the biopharma industry’s M&A activity. Behind the healthcare behemoth are BioNTech, Amgen and Roche in terms of gross cash balance, the firm determined.
All together, large-cap pharmas included in the analysis have about $188 billion on hand to spend, Leerink reported.

“Over the next year, we expect robust activity to continue, because many large-cap biopharma companies are hungry for M&A,” Leerink said. Indeed, the only company in the analysis to definitively say no to M&A is Genmab, which has said the near-term focus is on deleveraging.
Pharma’s total firepower is down slightly from the $199 billion that was recorded at the end of June 2025 due to a flurry of deals that have spread across the sector. So far this year pharma companies have spent $97 billion across 28 deals, according to Leerink. This is well above the annual mean from 2009 through 2025, when pharmas averaged 19 total deals and $69 billion spent.
“We have also seen more mid-size biopharma companies step up and pursue substantial acquisitions for the first time,” Leerink wrote. Inflammation and immunology (I&I), oncology, rare disease and central nervous system (CNS) have all seen major deals, while business development in cardiovascular or metabolic disease has declined.
Many major pharmas have significant debt levels, which can constrain deal activity. But Leerink doesn’t think this will greatly limit acquisitions in the sector. Bristol Myers Squibb, Novartis and GSK also have high debt but maintain flexibility.
AbbVie has the highest net debt balance at around $60 billion, but Leerink still believes the company has plenty of leverage to execute. And AbbVie’s leadership is among those executives signaling that a major transaction is possible, Leerink wrote.
“We always said we’re not unwilling to pursue a late stage, even an on-market opportunity if it fits,” CEO Rob Michael said at the Morgan Stanley Annual Global Healthcare Conference in September. He pointed to differentiated assets in immunology, oncology, neuroscience, aesthetics or obesity as possibilities.
“The lens, again, is on those key growth drivers, and we have the financial wherewithal,” Michael continued. “We have plenty of capacity to be able to continue to execute deals, whether that is an early-stage opportunity that’s going to drive long-term growth, a late-stage asset or even on market.”

Also signaling a potential transaction over $10 billion are the leaders of Eli Lilly, Amgen, AstraZeneca and Merck.
Lilly has been the busiest pharma of the year, with 11 total deals conducted as of the end of the third quarter, for $31.7 billion spent so far. The company’s executives have been unabashed in expressing their desire for more deals, even after onboarding dozens of new programs already this year.
“As highlighted by all the new molecules we added to our pipeline through acquisitions, business development is an important component of our R&D strategy,” Dan Skovronsky, chief scientific and product officer, said in August during the company’s second quarter earnings call.
For future deals, Leerink expects Lilly to look for diversification beyond metabolic to areas such as I&I, CNS or oncology.
Over at J&J, CEO Joaquin Duato has said he wants to find more early-stage deals to bulk up the company’s position later in the decade. “We can achieve double-digit growth this decade without M&A,” he said in September at the Morgan Stanley meeting. “So our goal with M&A is to fortify our position to provide you the confidence that our growth is durable into the next decade.”

2027 BMW X3 M50 xDrive Receives a New Black Package and an Additional 44 HP in the United States

BMW of North America has announced that Christmas is arriving early for the nice BMW M Performance fans of the BMW X3 M50 xDrive crossover SUV, which gains a power upgrade to 437 horsepower and independently can also be equipped with a new Black Package.
The premium Bavarian automaker BMW has been pretty busy during October 2026, with BMW of North America reporting the third-quarter US deliveries that surged by 3.4%, faster than the overall premium segment. BMW continues to hold the crown in the segment in America and will finish the year on top with the new iX3, X5, and 7 Series now at dealerships.
They also announced completely new products, like the all-new first-ever BMW iX4 coupe-SUV or the flagship iX3 M60 xDrive packing no less than 603 ponies, while BMW Motorrad presented the new F 450 RR lightweight motorcycle. But the month isn’t over yet, so there’s another ace up BMW’s sleeve – the X3 M50 xDrive gains a new Black Package and 437 hp.
Christmas for BMW M Performance fans starts early in December 2026 when the 2027 BMW X3 M50 xDrive becomes available with a new optional Black Package with dedicated exterior and interior details. Also, the M Performance model comes with an upgraded 3.0-liter TwinPower Turbo inline-six engine, now adding 44 hp compared to the current model and churning out up to 437 hp independent of the new Black Package.
The company also announces interior enhancements for the whole X3 lineup, with a PVC Softskin surface for the area in front of the central display, a new stitching pattern for the instrument panel, plus additional ambient lighting added to the center-console storage compartment and the interior door handles. There’s a new glove-box opener and stainless-steel edge protectors for the cargo sill, while the X3 M50 xDrive Black Package models also receive Dark Silver door-sill finishers with a black M logo.
The 2027 BMW X3 M50 xDrive can be bundled with the new Black Package, which consists of motorsport-inspired exterior and interior elements: bespoke 22-inch Jet Black 1134M alloy wheels, M Sport brake calipers with a high-gloss black finish with a monochrome M logo, and high-gloss black M logos and model badges with silver outlines for the exterior.
Inside, the new pack adds black Alcantara elements, an embossed M logo into the Alcantara headrests, black Alcantara/Veganza upholstery with blue stitching and piping, M interior trim in an aluminum-carbon style, M seatbelts, and black floor mats with M-color flags. Some controls also have glass accents, while the M steering wheel gains a leather-covered airbag module dedicated to the Black Package.
The BMW X3 M50 xDrive has a new output level, thanks to the mild hybrid 3.0L gaining 44 hp to 437 hp along with an “enhanced exhaust system (that) gives the engine a deeper, more resonant sound.” Now the model can sprint to 60 mph in 4.3 seconds.
The base MSRP of the 2027 BMW X3 M50 xDrive is $67,500 sans $1,350 for destination and handling, and the Black Package adds another $3,800 on top of that.

Truckload broker Landstar System noted strong demand for its dry van and flatbed offerings on its third-quarter call with analysts on Tuesday. A tightened capacity backdrop and the buildout of data centers are shaping the favorable fundamentals. However, insurance claims activity clouded an otherwise solid result.
“You can look down the P&L and if you skip one line known as insurance and claims, you’d have a lot of good news to write home about,” said Landstar President and CEO Frank Lonegro.
Landstar ( NASDAQ: LSTR ) reported third-quarter earnings per share of $1.42, which was 24 cents below the consensus estimate. The miss was attributable to $13 million (29 cents per share) in adverse adjustments to claims reserves and $8 million (18 cents per share) in unfavorable developments on two prior-year claims.
The result was 20 cents better than the adjusted EPS result from a year ago, which excluded several non-recurring items .
Table: Landstar’s key performance indicators
Consolidated revenue was up 25% y/y to $1.51 billion, which was largely in line with the consensus estimate.
Total truck revenue increased 29% y/y to $1.41 billion as loads increased 3% and revenue per load jumped 25%. Higher diesel fuel prices, along with improving TL pricing, drove the yield increase. Revenue per load was up 7.5% from the second quarter .
Dry van loads increased 6% y/y, with revenue per load up 23%. Flatbed loads increased 4% y/y, with yield up 29%. Landstar noted elevated heavy-haul demand.
Total truck loads are up 7% y/y in October, with revenue per load 29% higher. Both metrics are running “slightly above” historical sequential trends. The company normally sees a slight increase in truck revenue from the third to the fourth quarter as both loads and revenue per load increase approximately 1%.
SONAR: Outbound Tender Rejection Index (OTRI.USA) for 2026 (blue shaded area), 2025 (yellow line), 2024 (green line) and 2023 (pink line). A proxy for truck capacity, the tender rejection index shows the number of loads being rejected by carriers. Current tender rejections show a tight truckload market. To learn more about SONAR, click here .
SONAR: National Truckload Index ( linehaul only – NTIL.USA) for 2026 (blue shaded area), 2025 (yellow line), 2024 (green line) and 2023 (pink line). The NTIL is based on an average of booked spot dry van loads from 250,000 lanes. The NTIL is a seven-day moving average of linehaul spot rates excluding fuel. Rates remain higher on a y/y comparison in October.
Landstar culled its approved carrier list from over 100,000 in 2022 to nearly 68,000 in the recent quarter. The bulk of the reductions occurred in 2023 and into 2024 to combat cargo theft. The decline was also the result of deteriorating TL market conditions, especially for owner operators. Landstar’s approved carrier list was up 5% sequentially in the third quarter.
Trucks provided by business capacity owners (BCOs) increased 165 units sequentially to 8,709. This was the largest sequential increase since the 2021 third quarter. The BCO truck count is up 22 units from the end of the third quarter. The BCO truck turnover rate improved 480 basis points y/y to 26.6%.
BCO revenue per mile—Landstar’s preferred metric for TL pricing as it excludes fuel surcharges—was up 23% y/y on dry van loads and up 19% y/y on flatbed shipments. BCO revenue per load was 10.9% higher sequentially in the period.
Landstar’s BCOs are owner-operators who haul almost exclusively for the company. Changes among this segment of capacity have historically signaled turns in the broader TL market.
Variable contribution, or net revenue, increased 25% y/y to $212 million. (The calculation measures revenue remaining after purchased transportation expenses and agent commissions are paid.) A variable contribution margin of 14% was 10 bps lower y/y.
The adjusted operating margin (as a percentage of variable contribution) declined 220 bps y/y to 30.9%.
Insurance and claims expenses (as a percentage of BCO revenue) increased 220 bps y/y to 9.4%. The expense line was up $22.3 million y/y (to $55.3 million) due to the aforementioned unfavorable claims items, totaling $21 million. However, Landstar’s accident frequency improved again, dropping to 0.57 DOT reportable accidents per million miles through the first nine months of the year.
A spike in nuclear verdicts has materially moved the expense line in recent years. In 2016, the company guided insurance expense to just 3.2% of BCO revenue.
Why it matters? Landstar’s commentary provides some insight on how the industry is adapting, following the Supreme Court’s broker liability ruling . Its third-quarter results highlight how claims volatility can offset improving freight fundamentals, especially as insurers and brokers continue to adjust to a tougher liability environment.

A clearly superior clinical profile, reasonable pricing and easy access has helped a handful of recently approved therapies achieve impressive launches.
“Some drug launches arrive quietly; others redraw the map,” according to Shikha Bhardwaj, associate consultant at DelveInsight.
Over the last year or so, biopharma has witnessed several products that have done just that. These medicines performed strongly right out of the gate, delivering sales and uptake numbers that easily beat analyst and investor expectations.
To maximize their chances of a blowout launch, companies should strive to develop drugs that not only stand above the rest in terms of safety and efficacy but also address a critical gap in the current landscape, Gregory Renza, managing director & senior biotechnology equity research analyst at Truist Securities, told BioSpace .
“The profile is now doing the selling, and the commercial build is designed around demand that already exists rather than demand that has to be created,” he said.
A good example of this is Revolution Medicines’ Rasonque, approved in August for pancreatic cancer, Renza said. “Pancreatic cancer has gone a very long time without meaningful innovation, and the Phase 3 result is unprecedented there,” he added, pointing to data released in April that demonstrated overall survival more than double placebo.
“Differentiation is the marketing,” Renza said. “The launches working today are those with categorically new profiles, not incrementally better ones.”
Other big launches this year, like Novo’s oral Wegovy and Insmed’s Brinsupri, follow this playbook of having a clearly superior clinical profile, bolstered by a strong evidence base, reasonable pricing and ready accessibility.
“The next generation of successful launches will need more than scientific novelty,” DelveInsight’s Bhardwaj said in an email interview. “They will require a defensible clinical advantage, a price payers can justify, evidence that holds up over time, and a launch strategy that turns approval into sustained access and adoption.”
Below, BioSpace examines five drug launches defying expectations.
Novo springs out of the gate with oral Wegovy
When Novo launched the oral version of its obesity drug Wegovy on Jan. 5, analysts weren’t expecting much. After all, the Danish drugmaker had fumbled a years-long lead in the GLP-1 game to Eli Lilly, which many now regard as the weight loss leader. And, at the time, Lilly’s competitor pill was just months behind.
But Novo took everyone by surprise. After just a week on the market, oral Wegovy reached almost 3,100 patients , a strong opening salvo that sent the pharma’s shares up 6.5%. During the pharma’s first quarter call in May, CEO Maziar Mike Doustdar claimed that, at least outside of vaccines, oral Wegovy has the “strongest launch in U.S. pharma.” At the time, Novo touted $355 million in sales for the pill’s first commercial quarter.

“Novo built the launch around access rather than promotion,” Bhardwaj told BioSpace . More than 70,000 pharmacies across the U.S. and at least nine telehealth providers carry the pill, she explained. With a starting price of $149 per month for self-paying patients, oral Wegovy is “a consumer product as much as a prescription drug.”
But the oral obesity story is far from closed. Q2 sales for oral Wegovy hit $496 million, 2% behind consensus expectations. Meanwhile, Lilly’s Foundayo—which costs between $139 and $349 per month —seems to be rebounding from a slow launch after its April approval and is gaining ground. In an Oct. 2 note tracking scripts for these obesity medicines, BMO Capital Markets noted that prescriptions for oral Wegovy declined 1% from the previous week, while Foundayo grew 20.5%. Lilly still lags Novo in overall uptake volume.
RevMed offers option for pancreatic cancer at last with Rasonque
After securing a speedy approval in August—just five weeks after filing, courtesy of the FDA’s Commissioner’s National Priority Voucher program—Revolution Medicines’ pancreatic cancer drug Rasonque is now on track to achieving “one of the top oncology launches of all time,” Leerink Partners forecasted in an Oct. 5 note.
While RevMed has yet to reveal official sales figures for Rasonque, Bhardwaj agrees with Leerink and expects initial uptake to be strong. There was “substantial pre-launch clinical exposure” for the drug, she explained. “Through an expanded-access program, more than 2,000 patients had already received the drug, giving a broad group of oncologists experience with its use before commercial launch.”
RevMed has set Rasonque’s list price at $39,800 for a 30-day supply—a “substantial cost,” she told BioSpace , though through commercial insurance, some patients could pay as little as $0 out of pocket. While such steep discounts could boost uptake, they are also likely to raise payer questions “of whether the drug’s clinical benefit justifies its price.”

On this front, RevMed appears to be in good standing. In April, the Phase 3 RASolute 302 study—which supported Rasonque’s approval—showed that the drug doubled overall survival versus chemotherapy in patients with metastatic pancreatic cancer who had undergone prior treatment. Overall survival was one of the trial’s primary endpoints, alongside progression-free survival, which Rasonque also met.
“An unprecedented efficacy profile can carry a price through both the regulatory and payer gates simultaneously,” Truist’s Renza noted.
Some uncertainties remain, however. In October, the FDA released data pointing to a lower objective response rate with Rasonque in patients carrying certain KRAS mutations, including the G12D variant. Analysts remain largely unperturbed; Truist Securities at the time noted that the finding represents “a small crack in the data” for Rasonque.
Gilead to go big or go home with HIV preventative Yeztugo
Gilead has set a high bar for its twice-year HIV pre-exposure prophylactic (PrEP) therapy Yeztugo: Hit blockbuster status —or rake in $1 billion in sales—in its first full calendar year on the market.
Approved in June 2025 , Yeztugo is a long-acting preventative treatment designed to be administered once every six months. The problem with such a long interval between doses is adherence : Patients may not return for their second or subsequent injections.
That doesn’t seem to be a problem yet for Yeztugo. During the pharma’s second quarter earnings call, Chief Commercial and Corporate Affairs Officer Johanna Mercier said there is a “high level of persistency” with Yeztugo: more than seven in 10 patients who were initially treated returned for their second dose. This rate is “well above other PrEP options,” Mercier claimed on the call.
Yeztugo continues to move toward its blockbuster goal for this year. In the first six months of 2026, the long-term injection made $397 million . BMO in an Oct. 9 note forecasted $282.3 million in Q3 earnings for the drug, based on script data.
In an Aug. 4 note, however, analysts at Mizuho Securities pointed out that, for the first time ever, Gilead’s PrEP portfolio crossed the $1 billion quarterly earnings mark. Yeztugo hit Q2 sales of $232 million, while Descovy , a daily preventative pill, brought in $801 million.

J&J, Protagonist race past the incumbents with oral Icotyde
Approved in March for plaque psoriasis, Johnson & Johnson and Protagonist Therapeutics’ IL-23 blocker Icotyde, designed to be taken orally daily, “breaks from the injectable model that has dominated moderate-to-severe psoriasis for two decades,” Aparna Thakur, assistant project manager at DelveInsight, told BioSpace in an email.
Top psoriasis treatments, such as AbbVie’s Humira , Novartis’ Cosentyx and J&J’s own product Stelara , require injections. There is an oral powerhouse in Bristol Myers Squibb’s Sotyktu —which Thakur calls “the leading existing oral psoriasis drug”—but this drug bowed to Icotyde in the Phase 3 ICONIC-ADVANCE 1 and 2 studies, according to a March 2025 readout .
“Early uptake has been fast,” Thakur said of Icotyde. In the third quarter, J&J reported that the pill has reached more than 20,000 patients, the pharma reported last week , though specific sales figures have not been revealed.
Icotyde’s launch is “tracking better than most/all launches in psoriatic diseases,” Tom Cavanaugh, executive VP and worldwide chairman of Innovative Medicine, said during the pharma’s earnings call.
But for Thakur, “the most important signal is who is using it.”

Capping off this list is Insmed’s Brinsupri, which in August 2025 became the first-ever FDA-approved therapy for bronchiectasis, a chronic lung disease characterized by thickened and scarred airways.
Brinsupri costs $88,000 per year. The drug “carries a rare-disease-style price, yet bronchiectasis affects hundreds of thousands of diagnosed patients in the U.S.,” Thakur noted. Medicines for such large populations typically launch at lower prices, she explained, which helps secure broad payer coverage.
Despite premium pricing, Brinsupri has been performing well. During its first commercial quarter—Q4 2025—Brinsupri brought in $144.6 million . The drug has continued to grow, hitting $309.2 million in the second quarter, a 49% quarter-on-quarter increase.
Mizuho Securities in an Aug. 13 note said that Insmed delivered “a blowout Brinsupri result.”
The biotech expects Brinsupri to keep growing and has projected full-year sales of $1.25 billion to $1.4 billion.
For Insmed, keeping patients on Brinsupri will be crucial to meeting the blockbuster goal, Thakur said. “Brinsupri’s benefit is fewer exacerbations over time, which patients cannot feel day to day, so those with side effects or no immediate change may stop even if the drug is working,” she said. “At $88,000 a year, each early dropout removes most of a patient’s expected revenue, so persistence matters as much as new starts.”

Android Auto for Phone Screens Is Back Thanks to This Free App
8 photos
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution
It’s back. Android Auto for phone screens is back. Not thanks to Google, which has no intention to re-release a version of Android Auto specifically optimized for mobile devices, but courtesy of a developer who released the whole project as a free app.
Before anything else, I just want to answer a question that everybody on reddit seems to have: why would anyone need such an app?
Android Auto is a phone projection system, meaning that your smartphone must be connected to a compatible car head unit to run the app. The mobile device is the brain of the system, while the head unit shows the UI and provides users with methods to interact with their apps, most commonly via touch.
However, the big requirement here isn’t the mobile device, which we all have in our pockets, but an Android Auto head unit in your car. Many new-generation vehicles do come with such head units, as Android Auto and CarPlay have become extremely popular in the automotive space. But at the same time, many older-generation vehicles lack this functionality, and the only options in this case are the more expensive aftermarket upgrades.
This means you must spend hundreds of dollars on stand-alone Android Auto screens or head unit upgrades that also come with another shortcoming: they need professional installation, so you’ll end up spending even more dollars.
That’s why Android Auto for phone screens was a fantastic idea.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution The dedicated app released by Google allowed users to turn their smartphones into ad-hoc Android Auto screens. Instead of having your phone connected to a head unit, the phone became the head unit, running the familiar Android Auto interface directly on its screen. Instead of just having Google Maps on your mobile phone, you could get the whole Android Auto, therefore avoiding the ridiculous costs of hardware upgrades.
Google changed its mind in 2022 when it decided to kill off Android Auto for phone screens . The company did not release a replacement, despite originally launching a driving mode in Google Maps, but this half-baked solution was gradually phased out.
So right now, users who want to run Android Auto on their phones directly have no official option. Third-party alternatives do exist, and this week, another project joined the club.
PhoneAuto is a free app that has no ads, doesn’t require an account, and “leaves nothing on your phone,” as the developer explains on reddit . The project is documented here on GitHub .
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution Compared to Android Auto for phones, which was a more limited experience, PhoneAuto brings the actual Android Auto experience to your mobile device. You get everything you’d get on a factory-installed head unit, including the app dashboard, the Coolwalk screen, and even the cellular signal icon.
It works in both portrait and landscape modes, and the developer explains that everything should work, including the assistant. So yes, it’s not a half-baked Android Auto version but the actual, fully-featured application that all of us already have in our cars.
While there are a bunch of small things that need further polishing - such as support for foldables - the application seemingly works properly. It’s not yet posted on the Google Play Store - though such a version is currently in review - so you must install it from GitHub.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution You’ll notice a January 19 expiration date, as the developer used a similar approach like the one you can find on TestFlight on iPhones. Beta builds expire, so you must either install a newer beta by then or switch to the Google Play Store version.
Setting up PhoneAuto on your mobile device involves enabling developer mode on Android Auto and starting the head unit server. You’ll also need to shut it down manually when you close the app.
Android Auto for phone screens has long been a very popular app that Google retired in its frenzy of killing off products that people loved. While the driving mode migrated from Google Assistant to Google Maps was supposed to replace it , nothing worked as simply as users expected from an Android Auto experience.
PhoneAuto and OpenHeadunit are restoring the functionality that Google should offer as a first-party experience, as it’s obvious that users need a way to run Android Auto without an actual head unit.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution Someone on reddit highlights the most obvious use case: on a motorcycle, when aftermarket upgrades aren’t even possible, so turning a mobile phone into a head unit with Android Auto, which is supposed to provide a safer way to interact with mobile apps and also get full-screen navigation and access to music, is the best choice.
Open Headunit has been around for a while, so PhoneAuto will probably survive, too, with the developer promising further updates that will improve the experience regardless of the phone brand and model. You need at least Android 13 to run the app - though it could also work on older versions, though this has not been verified - and no other requirements should prevent you from trying it out.

Three former employees of large pharmas, including Novo and Sanofi, share how they were let go. While they appreciated some aspects of their experiences, such as severance and outplacement resources, they criticized a lack of public transparency, a mishandled notification and puzzling outsourcing.
How Big Pharma companies handle job cuts matters to employees, as seen in responses to an ongoing BioSpace survey collecting layoff stories and during a recent interview. From how they got the news to the severance packages they received, three biopharma professionals discuss what they thought of the way their former employers handled their exits. Two also share how their subsequent job searches have gone.
Getting the news at home, lack of external transparency not ideal
A principal scientist who requested anonymity had a mixed experience being laid off by a Big Pharma company where he had worked for a decade. The pharma, which he preferred not to name, let him go in March as part of a structural reorganization, he told BioSpace in a recent interview. The company was expanding into newer modalities and downsized the one he was working on, closing two departments while consolidating operations into one site.
The scientist learned he was out of a job when a vice president visited the location where he worked, gathered everyone together and announced the layoffs, including the reason behind them. He got the news at home, as he was working remotely that day. Reflecting on that moment, he said he wishes he had been at the office.
“I would have much rather have been on-site because it would have been, obviously, difficult with your co-workers, but to have that kind of shared trauma together would have been better for me,” he explained.
Hearing the news in a group setting rather than one-on-one didn’t bother the scientist.
“I think it was just shocking, regardless,” he said.
What did bother him was the pharma not publicly announcing the layoffs, which he noted other companies have done when trimming their workforces. He noted that the only press release the business issued at that time focused on another matter. It felt, he said, like the pharma was perhaps trying to hide the cuts from the public.
While the scientist didn’t like that aspect of the layoffs, he was satisfied with his severance package. Those let go received around 10 weeks of salary plus additional pay based on years of service and age over a set number, he said. He ended up with almost six months of pay. On top of that, the company also paid out unused vacation time and covered health insurance for however long severance lasted.
It took the scientist six months to land his next position, at a biotech. He estimated that he applied for 20 to 30 openings and noted that he was a bit selective during his job search, with a preference for smaller companies for two reasons. First, he said, many friends and former colleagues had shifted from a pharma to a biotech and had told him about the benefits of such a move. Second, biotechs had more openings than large pharmas for someone at his level with his expertise.
“So, the search was focused on smaller companies just because that’s where a lot of the positions were,” he said. “But I think it was also a welcome change.”
Missed notification gives false hope on job security
One BioSpace survey respondent criticized how their former employer, Novo, handled recent layoffs. They were among the roughly 400 people the Danish pharma let go in early May at a Bloomington, Indiana, sterile fill/finish site previously owned by Catalent. Novo acquired the contract development and manufacturing organization (CDMO) in 2024 and now owns and operates the Bloomington location.
The respondent shared that when Novo told employees it would announce layoffs in a month, people recalled how the last workforce reduction at that site, when Catalent owned and operated it, had gone. Some had learned they’d lost their jobs not from their employer but when an employee outplacement services company contacted them. Others had found out when their badges didn’t work at the office. Because the Bloomington site’s HR team was still the same, the respondent noted, there were low expectations for how the latest job cuts would go.
“And sure enough, despite the company change, there was a screw up,” they wrote.
Employees were told layoff calls would be from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m., and most people were allowed to work remotely so they could be at home if they got a call, the respondent noted. Those who didn’t hear from Novo by 8 p.m. thought they were safe. That group included the survey respondent, who had previously escaped a handful of layoffs at the Bloomington site.
However, when they went to check Microsoft Teams on their work phone, their access to Teams through Novo didn’t work. They contacted their manager on LinkedIn and, shortly after, learned they had been let go, along with their entire department. For some reason, the respondent’s name had not been on the HR team’s list of people to call.
In addition to the way they learned they had been let go, the respondent took issue with Novo’s explanation for the workforce reduction.
Nobody clearly stated the reason for the layoff. We got the typical corporate mumbo jumbo and heard the word ‘sustainable’ too many times.
Former Novo employee
“Nobody clearly stated the reason for the layoff,” they wrote. “We got the typical corporate mumbo jumbo and heard the word ‘sustainable’ too many times.”
They noted, however, that at the end of the day, an FDA warning letter had led to lost CDMO business Novo had inherited from Catalent.
The agency’s November 2025 letter summarized significant violations of current good manufacturing practice regulations for finished pharmaceuticals at the Bloomington site. The FDA also issued complete response letters to Incyte, Regeneron and Scholar Rock, companies that were using the facility for fill/finish activities.
Job outsourcing amidst heavy workload proves frustrating
Another survey respondent expressed frustration with the reason they lost their position at Sanofi. In March 2025, their manager told them the pharma was outsourcing part of their job, and HR felt the employee wouldn’t have enough work left to justify the headcount. However, the respondent wrote, the responsibility was a minor one.
“In reality,” they added, “our whole team had been working to the point of burnout for over a year, and had every indication that this trend would continue for the foreseeable future. My manager had actually been trying to get 1-2 more headcount.”
Sanofi did handle one aspect of the layoffs in a way the respondent appreciated. They noted that they received a generous severance package and access to a career coaching and resume revising service that has helped them get job applications “past the ubiquitous bots” and secure some interviews.
However, in their survey comments left in August, over a year after their layoff, the respondent wrote that they had not yet landed a job. They described a frustrating search process that included having countless opportunities cancelled after they applied or interviewed. They also noted that hiring managers said they wanted to bring them back for second interviews but then ghosted them for months.

Photo: Cavco Industries
Tiny living has been around for decades, but it has never been more popular than it is these days. It seems that the movement has entered into a new era, having picked up more steam lately due to real estate constraints and people's desire to live more intentionally.
Now, tiny houses, be they on wheels or on foundation, are posed as highly practical alternatives for individuals looking to escape the financial weight of mortgages or high rent. But many of those intrigued by the idea of living in a tiny house to lead a simpler life and carry less financial burden are worried they’ll have to sacrifice too much space or comfort.
If you, too, have these kinds of concerns, you’ll love the Harbor tiny house. This slightly oversized tiny home has all the residential amenities you’re accustomed to and feels right the moment you walk through the front door. Designed as a cabin on wheels, it offers both the simplicity and cozy charm of a traditional tiny home and the functionality and comfort of a full-size dwelling, making downsizing feel like an upgrade.
Harbor is built by Fairmont Homes, a manufacturer with decades of experience in the housing industry. Founded in 1971 in Nappanee, Indiana, the company became part of Cavco Industries in 2015 but it continued to create beautiful and functional compact homes whose construction uses high-end residential materials like finished drywall, steel I-beams, OSB sheathing, and robust fiberglass insulation. This thing alone is enough to understand that their homes are made for more than just occasional weekend stays.
Photo: Cavco Industries Stretching 45 feet (13.7 meters) long and 11.5 feet (3.5 meters) wide, Harbor is a park model tiny home that boasts a roomier layout compared to traditional homes on wheels and is designed to fit your real, everyday life with an inviting lounge with a built-in entertainment center, a spacious U-shaped kitchen with dining space, two downstairs bedrooms, and a large bathroom.
In total, you get 505 square feet (just under 47 square meters) of living space, with no ladders to climb or low-ceiling lofts to navigate, making everyday living more comfortable. Of course, a “tiny” home of this size comes with a trade-off: it’s less convenient to move than a conventional tiny house on wheels.
Due to its generous dimensions, it would require professional hauling and special permits to be towed on public roads, but it still remains an appealing downsizing solution for people who want a more permanent living arrangement and intend to keep it parked in one location for longer periods of time.
With Harbor, the emphasis is clearly less on taking it everywhere and more on making the interior feel comfortable and complete. And if we take a look at the picture gallery and the floor plan, it indeed seems like a complete home. The two-bedroom layout makes it suitable for family life, and the full suite of residential amenities means it’s well-equipped for full-time occupancy.
Photo: Cavco Industries This park model has not one but two entrances, and the main one is a double glass sliding door that leads directly into the central living room. Open and fitted with an L-shaped sofa, a coffee table, and an entertainment center, it feels like a proper lounge in a conventional home. The entertainment wall, which integrates a TV and a fireplace with a wooden mantel, is strategically positioned between two expanses of glass that provide beautiful views and bring in ample natural light.
The living room is seamlessly connected to the right with a huge U-shaped kitchen that wraps around the front area of the house. It features ample base and upper hardwood cabinets and a standalone dining table in the center, which could also serve as a kitchen island for additional counter space. A large front window and several transom windows keep the space luminous, while the neutral styling and stainless steel appliances give it a contemporary appearance.
Photo: Cavco Industries Fit for a chef, this cooking space includes a large, residential refrigerator, a full range, a range hood, a microwave, and a farmhouse-style stainless steel sink.
The secondary entrance door offers direct access to the more private areas of the house. It opens into a hallway with doors to the bathroom and the two separate bedrooms. The master bedroom is located at the very rear of the house and has all the attributes of a conventional room, with a comfortable bed, space to walk around it, nightstands, and plenty of storage solutions, including overhead cubbies and a full wardrobe. There is also space for a wall-mounted TV, while two windows keep the room luminous and airy.
Photo: Cavco Industries The other bedroom is a bit smaller and is designed for kids with built-in bunk beds and a closet. Next to the bunk room is the bathroom, which is compact but well-equipped. It features a fully-tiled standing shower with glass door, a vanity with an elongated counter, a toilet, and a mirrored medicine cabinet. Harbor also includes a dedicated space for a washer/dryer with hookups already available, a floor-to-ceiling general closet, and a furnace closet, adding more convenience for full-time living.
Built on a heavy-duty quad-axle trailer, the Harbor park model tiny home features a modern exterior with Royal Dutch lap vinyl siding, a metal roof, ventilated soffits, and breathable mesh underbelly. This model is part of Cavco Homes’ Country Manor series and is only available in Canada, with pricing depending on the dealer you choose to work with.

WEX is expanding its use of artificial intelligence and digital payment technology for trucking fleets, announcing a partnership with Euclid AI on Tuesday aimed at automating back-office operations and reducing costs for over-the-road carriers.
The announcement came during the WEX OTR Summit in Jacksonville, Florida, where Cade Mund, senior director and head of product for WEX OTR, outlined the company’s technology roadmap for 2026 and 2027, including cardless fueling, modernized fleet management software and AI-powered purchasing tools .
Under the agreement, WEX (NYSE: WEX ) and San Francisco-based Euclid AI will work together to bring AI agents designed specifically for trucking operations to WEX’s OTR customers.
Euclid said its technology has enabled fleet managers to handle five to 10 times more work while reducing costs per transaction by 80% to 90% in existing production deployments.
“Our customers are looking for practical ways to take cost and complexity out of running a fleet, and AI agents built specifically for trucking are a significant step forward,” said Tim Hampton, senior vice president and general manager of WEX OTR, in a news release .
Hampton said the collaboration would extend WEX’s services beyond its existing payments and fleet management products .
AI agents target trucking paperwork, compliance
Euclid’s technology is designed to automate repetitive administrative tasks that consume time and resources at trucking companies.
Its Precision Agents can process bills of lading, proof-of-delivery documents, driver qualification records and compliance paperwork, according to the announcment.
The agents can also manage communications involving drivers, customers and dispatchers, including shipment updates, document requests and follow-up messages.
Other applications include automating multistep workflows, such as moving freight documentation through billing or managing compliance renewals.
Euclid CEO Ahmad Kakar said the partnership would make the company’s technology available to WEX’s OTR customer base.
“We’ve already delivered major results for the largest carriers in the country,” Kakar said in a statement. “Together, we’re putting that same power in the hands of WEX OTR customers.”
WEX did not announce a specific deployment schedule or pricing structure for the new AI services.
WEX expands cardless fueling network
During his presentation, titled “Fueling the Future 2.0: The WEX OTR Product & Payments Roadmap,” Mund said the company’s strategy centers on making fuel purchases more seamless, intelligent and connected to other fleet operations.
“I believe that the future of fueling is a frictionless experience for our customers,” Mund said.
He said WEX recently launched its cardless fueling network, allowing drivers to purchase fuel without relying on a physical payment card.
The network is operating at Pilot Flying J, Love’s, TravelCenters of America, Maverik and SCI terminals, according to Mund, with additional merchants expected to join.
While WEX wants to reduce reliance on physical fuel cards, Mund said traditional cards will remain part of the payments ecosystem.
“I think plastic is going to be around for a while,” he said. “I don’t think it’s just going to go away.”
Fleet management modernization continues
WEX is also upgrading its eManager fleet management platform, which Mund acknowledged has become outdated.
“There’s a customer quote that I heard this year that said eManager, you can do pretty much everything if you can find it,” Mund told attendees.
The company is redesigning the system to simplify navigation and improve access to fleet management functions.
WEX has also introduced a unified authentication system intended to allow customers to access multiple services through a single login, including fuel management, permitting and fuel tax tools.
Other improvements include application programming interfaces that allow carriers to integrate fuel pricing and discount data into their own optimization systems.
Looking ahead to 2027, Mund said WEX plans to continue expanding cardless fueling, modernizing payment products and incorporating AI into fleet management decisions.
Potential applications include monitoring transactions, recommending changes to fuel card settings and helping process requests for purchases outside a driver’s normal fueling network.
“AI can help make those decisions and perform those actions on your behalf,” Mund said.
Why it matters: WEX says AI-powered automation and digital payments could help trucking fleets reduce administrative costs, streamline operations and improve efficiency amid tight margins.

Aston Martin Reveals the Valhalla Spider: It's Formula 1 With the Wind in Your Hair
25 photos
Photo: Aston Martin
Aston Martin has officially unveiled the Valhalla Spider. The drop-top sibling of the coupe is making its global debut at the 2026 Concours at Wynn Las Vegas as the brand' first mid-engined open-cockpit production supercar. Arriving nearly two years after the debut of the coupe, the convertible cuts off the roof while preserving design and performance specs.
It took Aston Martin ages to reveal the production Valhalla based on the AM-R 003 Concept unveiled back in March 2019 at the Geneva Motor Show. Production hurdles, redesign, and re-engineering pushed the debut date years after the original schedule. The Valhalla Coupe wasn't ready until December 2024.
Fast forward to 2026, here is the Spider version. Let's do numbers first, because that is what we are all here for, right? Long story short, the all-new Aston Martin Valhalla Spider is powered by the same flat-plane crank 4.0-liter twin-turbocharged V8, working alongside three electric motors.
While the V8 pumps out 817 horsepower (828 metric horsepower) and 627 pound-feet (850 Newton meters) of torque, the electric trio brings 247 horsepower (251 metric horsepower) and 184 pound-feet (250 Newton meters) of torque.
Photo: Aston Martin Two of the three electric motors are mounted on the front axle and power the front wheels independently, allowing the car to vary power to each front wheel to maximize cornering grip. The third electric motor sits on the rear axle, sending power exclusively to the rear wheels.
Combined, the setup puts down 1,064 horsepower (1,079 metric horsepower) and 811 pound-feet (1,100 Newton meters). That is enough to make the supercar rocket from zero to hero (0 to 60 mph or 0 to 97 kph) in just 2.4 seconds on its way to a top speed of 217 mph (350 kph), just like the coupe, despite the weight gain due to the extra reinforcement that drop-tops usually come with.
Those numbers make the Valhalla Spider the fastest open-cockpit car Aston Martin has ever built. Because yes, the brand's first mid-engined open-cockpit production supercar comes with the exact same uncompromising performance, which translates to aerodynamics, speed, and brutal acceleration metrics.
An eight-speed dual-clutch automatic transmission puts the power down through all four corners with the help of the e-AWD system. The gearbox features an integrated e-reverse function, where the electric motors handle reversing, eliminating a mechanical reverse gear to keep the gearbox lighter.
Photo: Aston Martin The Valhalla , be it a coupe or a drop-top, serves as a direct pipeline for F1-derived technology borrowed from the Aston Martin Aramco Formula 1 Team. Developed in collaboration with Aston Martin Performance Technologies (AMPT), its design focuses heavily on shaving lap times with the help of active aerodynamics, advanced materials, and motorsport ergonomics.
The core structure of the hyper-lightweight carbon fiber tub is manufactured using a combination of Resin Transfer Moulding (RTM) and F1-grade autoclave tech to keep weight under control. Furthermore, the front end sits on an F1-style pushrod suspension, featuring inboard dampers to optimize weight distribution and lower the center of gravity.
The Valhalla integrates F1-style aerodynamics. It sports wings hidden from view at the front and rear to actively modulate their angle of attack as they serve as either a Drag Reduction System (DRS) or angle upward to produce downforce. That results in 1,323 pounds (600 kilograms) of downforce at the back with the roof fitted.
In the meantime, the underfloor sports a concave surface and small slotted louvers, the so-called vortex generators, designed to act like mini diffusers and pull high-speed air out from under the car to form an incredible low-pressure ground effect.
Photo: Aston Martin The driver sits in what Aston Martin calls the "Amphitheater" interior, mimicking the cockpit of the Valkyrie hypercar. That translates to a heavily reclined seating position, also replicating the ergonomics of the Aston Martin F1 race cars driven by Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll.
The driver gets a new carbon fiber Touring Seat, offered as standard on the Valhalla Spider for enhanced comfort and easier entry and exit. Buyers can go for the original carbon fiber seat of the coupe at no extra cost. The dihedral doors keep their ground in the convertible, now featuring a small increase in the curvature of the door glass top edge.
While the Valhalla coupe 's snorkel intake is built directly into the center of its fixed roof to supply vital cooling ducts for the intercoolers and the Hot-V turbo layout, the Spider's snorkel migrated to the rear deck spine right behind the seats, 35 millimeters higher so that it can remain fully functional even when the roof panel is removed.
When the carbon fiber roof is off, a three-piece clip-on wind deflector can be clipped directly onto the upper edge of the windshield frame to protect passengers from severe buffeting, while channeling the airflow straight back into the mid-mounted engine snorkel on the rear deck and making sure the V8 is never deprived of oxygen. The Valhalla Spider owner also goes home with a rain cover for static use.
Photo: Aston Martin Deliveries will start in the third quarter of 2027. Aston Martin hasn't revealed any pricing details just yet. The Valhalla Coupe was a $1,051,000 deal when new. The Spider is estimated to start around the $1.5 million mark.
The British firm rolled out only 999 coupes, so the Spider is also expected to be produced in low numbers to keep its exclusivity in a segment where it battles the Lamborghini Revuelto Roadster nd the Ferrari SF90 XX Spider .

The U.S. Department of Transportation announced $498 million for 35 port projects across 19 states, including dock replacements, cargo equipment, rail connections and terminal upgrades.
What’s Related
The awards come through the Maritime Administration’s Port Infrastructure Development Program and cover coastal seaports, Great Lakes ports and inland river ports. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the investment aims to improve supply chains and lower shipping costs.
The announcement highlights seven projects, ranging from a new seafood pier in Maine to dock replacements in Alaska and infrastructure monitoring technology in Texas .
RELATED: DOT Awards $1.73B in Infrastructure Grants. Here’s Where It’s Going
Where the money is going
Whittier, Alaska: $50,593,488. The city will replace the DeLong Dock, add a seasonal floating dock and a dock manager building, and acquire three pedestal cranes and an integrated tug and barge.
Port Everglades, Florida: $30,750,000. The Fort Lauderdale port will strengthen its liquid bulk terminal and widen the slip to accommodate larger ships. The work is intended to help maintain critical fuel operations during severe weather.
Rockport Harbor, Maine: $698,750. The harbor will build a 20-by-30-foot fixed timber pier to improve seafood transfers from vessels to trucks . Construction includes 12 timber piles, marine-grade connectors, and a vessel fendering system.
Red Wing Port Authority, Minnesota: $10,161,985. The authority will rebuild its barge loading system, conveyors , electric winch, and dust collection systems. The project will increase cargo throughput and raise loading infrastructure above the Mississippi River floodplain.
North Carolina State Ports Authority, Morehead City: $11,250,000. The project includes a 75-foot pile-supported concrete deck for heavy-lift cargo, a new crane rail and two on-dock rail extensions. Funding also covers security technology and optical character recognition software for tracking.
Port Freeport, Texas: $9,412,500. The port will replace a 25-year-old bulk rice loader, install storage racks, and move the rice storage shed’s southern wall to expand berthing space.
Port of Corpus Christi Authority, Texas: $7,153,376. The authority will acquire a digital twin, or virtual model, along with sensors and software to monitor pipeline, rail, road, and waterway infrastructure. Equipment includes laser scanning technology, sonar, high-definition cameras, and transponders.
MARAD says the program aims to reduce shipping time and costs through port improvements. The release does not provide construction start dates or completion schedules for the highlighted projects.
More DOT funding for freight infrastructure
The latest port funding adds to DOT grants announced this year for rail improvements, truck parking, and other transportation projects.
A separate $2.3 billion grant will fund 105 rail projects across 45 states and Washington, D.C. The awards include freight bridge repairs, track upgrades, and $30 million to rehabilitate and expand Texas City Terminal Railway’s rail yard and realign a port vehicle entrance.
Truck parking is another focus , with $200 million awarded to 14 projects in 12 states. Projects include approximately 275 truck spaces near the Port of Savannah and about 140 truck spaces and 50 container staging positions at the Port of Wilmington.
Through its BUILD program , DOT also awarded $1.73 billion for 127 transportation projects. That funding included $136.8 million for port infrastructure and $87.7 million for freight rail, along with investments in roads, bridges, and truck parking.

Kaye/Bassman’s Michael Pietrack explores the guilt and grief executives feel when their direct reports are downsized and provides a strategy that helps both the leader and the people who need new jobs.
A few weeks ago, I was on the phone with a biopharma executive who recently had to announce the downsizing of her team. Her own role was safe for the time being, but she was sure it was not for long. She told me her plan for moving forward. She was going to wait until every single person on her team landed somewhere new before she started looking for her own opportunity. It sounded noble. It sounded like the kind of leadership we say we want more of. It just wasn’t the right strategy.
She asked me if, as a recruiter, I’d ever seen a whole team, including the manager, land somewhere together, intact, like someone just cut and pasted the org chart onto a new company. I told her that was a nice thought, but nothing I had observed before. As much as her team might like to work together again, the chance of them all getting hired at the same new company was slim.
My answer disappointed her, and then she explained how much the downsizing was bothering her. She knew these people. She’d recruited most of them herself and gotten close enough to know about their families. She was fully aware of what was at stake for each person, and frankly, she was sick about it, so she wanted to make sure everyone was securely in a new role before she was.
I questioned her plan, asking her if waiting was really the loyal move, or whether getting herself placed quickly served her team better. A leader with a new seat can do something a leader still job-hunting can’t. She can open doors from the inside. The situation reminded me of a mother who wouldn’t serve herself a meal until everyone else at the table had eaten. It’s a loving instinct, but it’s also a losing one if she starves herself out of the one job opportunity that could feed everybody else faster.
I explained to the executive that there’s a name for what people feel when they survive a layoff: survivor’s guilt. Remorse sets in from still having a job when those around you don’t. What she had wasn’t quite that, though. I told her it was more like leader’s guilt. Though she had not decided the layoff, she’d had to announce it. Plus, she was the one who had recruited these people into the seats that just disappeared. In her mind, she had gotten them into this. She felt guilty for an outcome that was never hers to control. There was only one real fix for her leader’s guilt, and that was the one I mentioned above: Land somewhere where she could bring people with her.
I told her the term I hear people using in industry is “coat tailing,” where junior people ride the coattails of a strong leader from job to job. I think of it more like drafting, the way a smaller car tucks in behind a semi and rides in the pocket of air it clears. Most of her team had already done that when they had followed her into this job in the first place. The fastest way she could help them do it again was to find her own seat as soon as possible.
When I told her that, she admitted something else. She wasn’t emotionally ready to interview with another company. I told her that made sense. It’s the same as when someone loses a dog, and a well-meaning friend says, “Just get a new puppy.” It’s almost like she was grieving the death of something she loved. Not just her team, but the company itself, the one she’d poured years into, the one that didn’t really exist anymore, not the way she’d known it.
However genuine those feelings were, I explained that grieving doesn’t mean putting life on pause. She could work through those feelings while building whatever came next. She didn’t have to wait to interview until she felt ready. The guilt and the grief didn’t have to resolve first. Moving forward was the fastest way to help the people she wanted to help.
I added a balancing statement, that even if she started looking for herself first, it was no guarantee she would land before everyone else. It could happen, but it was unpredictable. Executive interview processes take longer than individual contributor searches. Who would get a job first, them or her, remained to be seen, but at least she would put herself in a position to get a role and let her former team coattail.
Before we hung up, I said it simply: Don’t wait. I encouraged her to go after her next role with everything she had while also helping her former team with calls and introductions. Action would ease guilt and grief. And, if she landed somewhere new that could also employ people from her old team, she would have done right by herself and by those hoping to work with her again.

Port Houston recorded an 11% year-over-year increase in container volumes in September, fueled by stronger imports and improving export activity through its Bayport and Barbours Cut container terminals.
The port handled 376,419 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) during the month, compared with 337,659 TEUs during the same month in 2025, according to figures presented during the Oct. 21 Port Commission meeting.
Through the first nine months of 2026, Port Houston handled 3.35 million TEUs, up 2% from 3.27 million TEUs during the same period last year.
Loaded container imports rose 16% year over year in September to 174,189 TEUs, while loaded exports increased 2% to 132,009 TEUs.
Port Houston CEO Charlie Jenkins said September’s performance represented a significant improvement after a challenging start to 2026.
“We had a pretty rough start to the year,” Jenkins told commissioners, adding that recent cargo activity had improved the port’s outlook heading into the final quarter.
Ryan Mariacher, the port’s chief operations officer, said container activity at Bayport and Barbours Cut continued to benefit from stronger import demand, while export volumes began accelerating toward the end of September.
“The growth at Bayport and Barber’s Cut for the month was largely driven by import s,” Mariacher said during the meeting.
He added that the second half of September and first half of October brought a long-anticipated surge in export volumes.
Port officials said ocean carriers and shippers expect the stronger export activity to continue in the near term, potentially supporting additional freight movements through Houston’s container terminals.
Houston container imports outperform national trends
John Mosley, Port Houston’s chief commercial officer, said import demand remained unusually strong during the third quarter, traditionally the peak shipping season as retailers prepare for year-end sales.
“This year has been unusually high with Port Houston outpacing the rest of the country,” Mosley told commissioners.
He cited National Retail Federation Port Tracker data showing Houston among the strongest-performing major U.S. container gateways for import growth.
Loaded imports through Port Houston increased 6% year to date through September, compared with a much weaker national import market, according to Mosley.
The port’s September figures showed loaded imports increasing to 1.56 million TEUs through the first nine months, compared with 1.47 million TEUs during the same period in 2025.
Mosley said the port was cautiously optimistic that exports would continue strengthening during the fourth quarter.
Port officials have been meeting with major international ocean carriers to discuss additional shipping capacity, improved terminal throughput and opportunities to expand services.
Eric Casey, Port Houston’s chief operating officer, said the port launched a new container and refrigerated cargo service in September and was negotiating additional services.
“Commercially, we started a new container and reefer service in September, and more services are being negotiated today, so we are growing,” Casey said.
The port’s September 2026 comparative statistics also showed a 31% increase in empty container exports, to 55,963 TEUs, compared with 42,782 TEUs a year earlier.
The increase in empty equipment movements underscores the importance of container repositioning as ocean carriers balance import and export demand.
Vessel traffic increases as cargo volumes rebound
Port Houston recorded 750 vessel movements at its public terminals during September, up 10% from 681 a year earlier.
Through September, vessel movements totaled 6,562, an 8% increase from 6,096 during the same period last year.
Barge activity also increased, with 181 movements in September, up 23% year over year.
The higher vessel activity coincided with stronger cargo throughput at the port’s public terminals, where total revenue tonnage increased 15% year over year to 4.88 million tons.
Year-to-date cargo tonnage reached 42.37 million tons, up 2% from the same period in 2025.
Port officials also highlighted the completion of Port Houston-led portions of Project 11, the Houston Ship Channel expansion project designed to accommodate larger vessels and improve navigation.
The project widened a section of the Houston Ship Channel through Galveston Bay from 530 feet to 700 feet, allowing larger ships to move more efficiently and reducing daylight navigation restrictions.
Jenkins said Port Houston was also advancing planning for Project 12, the next major expansion of the Houston Ship Channel, while considering ways to accelerate individual improvements to maintain the competitiveness of its container terminals .
He noted that Port Houston previously accelerated channel improvements serving Bayport and Barbours Cut rather than waiting for the broader federal project schedule.
Steel imports surge 181% in September
Beyond containers, Port Houston reported a sharp increase in steel shipments, reflecting stronger activity tied to construction, manufacturing and energy infrastructure projects.
Steel imports totaled 539,993 tons in September, up 181% from 192,351 tons a year earlier.
Combined steel imports and exports exceeded 581,000 tons, the port’s strongest monthly steel performance since May 2022, according to operations officials.
Port Houston also reported its first consecutive months exceeding 500,000 tons of steel in more than a decade.
General cargo volumes have also increased, with officials pointing to rail-bound project cargo, including large electrical equipment and infrastructure components, as an important contributor to growth.

Körber is acquiring a stake in NAiSE, a German software company whose fleet management platform coordinates warehouse robots and manually operated industrial vehicles from different manufacturers . Announced Oct. 22, the investment expands the companies' existing partnership .
What’s Related
The companies plan to connect NAiSE’s platform more closely with Körber’s warehouse technology and develop additional uses for the software. Körber did not disclose the investment amount or the size of its stake.
Founded in 2017, NAiSE had financed its business independently before the investment. Its software brings automated guided vehicles, autonomous mobile robots and manually operated industrial trucks into a shared system to coordinate material movement in warehouses and factories.
“We deliberately chose a partner that respects our independence and also helps us scale internationally,” said Kai Przybysz-Herz, co-founder and CEO of NAiSE. The company will continue working with other system integrators and vehicle manufacturers.
Connecting vehicles from different systems
The software addresses a practical challenge for warehouses using equipment from several manufacturers: coordinating vehicles that otherwise work through separate systems. NAiSE says its platform provides a common layer for managing those fleets.
According to NAiSE, its Fleet Manager brings mobile robots, forklifts , tugger trains, and other manually operated vehicles into one system. A central control layer coordinates tasks across the different vehicles, giving managers a shared view of the fleet.
The platform also links fleet management to transport orders, traffic coordination and warehouse management . Its Order Manager translates requests from business and warehouse systems into transport tasks and assigns work across manually operated vehicles and autonomous robots.
NAiSE says its Traffic Manager coordinates vehicle movement and infrastructure through shared control logic. The software provides real-time visibility , routing and simulation tools to plan how mixed fleets move through a facility.
Working with existing warehouse software
Körber says NAiSE’s integration tools connect vehicles and systems regardless of which warehouse management, execution, or control software a customer uses. Those systems manage inventory , organize work, and direct equipment inside a facility.
The companies intend to deepen the connection between NAiSE and Körber’s warehouse products while continuing to develop the platform for production logistics . Existing robot-manufacturer partnerships will also remain available to joint and new customers.
“Körber brings deep industrial experience, a global customer network and a genuine understanding of entrepreneurial thinking,” added Przybysz-Herz.

YouTube on CarPlay No More: Popular App APTV No Longer Working After iOS 27.2
18 photos
Photo: Florin Profir/autoevolution
YouTube isn’t officially supported on Android Auto and CarPlay (not yet, at least), but unofficially, users have been able to access Google’s video platform for quite some time. One of the apps that made this possible on CarPlay has stopped working recently, and the developer says Apple’s latest iPhone update is the one to blame.
APTV is an app whose main selling point is controversial, to say the least. The application allows users to watch YouTube through a browser, essentially unlocking the functionality that Apple has until now kept locked.
The iPhone maker paved the way for video apps on CarPlay with the release of iOS 26.4, but so far, video app support still hasn’t reached the point where users can install YouTube and start watching videos in their cars.
This is why APTV has become so popular. With a plug-and-play approach, APTV allowed users to install the app from the App Store, point the browser to YouTube, and load a video. It was that easy, and the app even offered additional functionality like logging in with a Google account.
The most controversial part was the video watching capabilities while the car was in motion. Users have reported a mixed experience on this front, and while some said that APTV did not allow them to watch the videos when they started driving, others claimed that the playback continued. This mixed experience could also be linked to the CarPlay head unit, as a factory-installed system is more likely to prompt a block when motion is detected.
Apple shipped iOS 27.2 this week, and it turns out that APTV stopped working altogether. The reason, the app developers say, is that the update has disabled this functionality on iPhones.
“Apple has disabled this CarPlay video functionality in iOS 27.2, so this is not an issue that we can fix through an APTV software update,” the developers told an app user. The only fix, they claim, is downgrading an iPhone to the previous iOS version.
The reason invoked by the APTV team doesn’t provide more context, but it looks like the “disabled functionality” that the devs highlight is actually a streaming video vulnerability that Apple has patched in iOS 27.2. I have reached out to both companies for additional information and will update the article if and when I hear back.
Video apps are still coming to Android Auto and CarPlay, and right now, it looks like Google users are more likely to get their hands on these apps first. Google has already announced support for video apps in the spring of this year, with the Cielo update for Android Auto expected to go live later this year or in the first quarter of 2027.
When this new app category is unlocked on Android Auto, users will be allowed to watch videos when their cars are stationary. An audio-only mode will be available in apps that support it, thereby blocking video when cars start moving.

Bosch has unveiled the latest generation of its popular Active Line Plus electric bicycle motor, bringing more power, less weight, and a significantly smaller footprint to one of the company’s most widely used drive systems.
The new motor is designed primarily for everyday riders, including commuters, recreational cyclists, and those who want a comfortable e-bike that can handle everything from city streets to weekend trail rides.
And while it isn’t Bosch’s most powerful motor, the upgrades are fairly substantial.
The new Active Line Plus now produces up to 600 watts of peak power and 60 Nm of torque, along with a maximum pedal assistance level of 340%. That’s enough to give riders a healthy boost when accelerating away from traffic lights or climbing hills, without necessarily turning their everyday commuter into an overpowered mountain bike.

Like its predecessor, the motor is designed for Class 1 electric bicycles in the US, providing pedal assistance up to 20 mph (32 km/h) without a throttle.
Remember, the Active Line motor is the drive system model that many e-bike companies use for their modestly performing e-bikes . It gives good power and control, combined with all the tech we’ve come to expect from Bosch, but it isn’t the motor e-bike makers use when they need an electric mountain bike to scale a steep mountainous trail.
Smaller, lighter, and quieter
Perhaps even more interesting than the increased power is what Bosch has done to the motor’s physical design.
The company developed a new two-stage gearbox that helps reduce the motor’s overall volume by 17% while shaving approximately 1.1 lb (0.5 kg) off its weight.
The new drive unit now tips the scales at around 6 lb (2.7 kg), making it easier for bicycle manufacturers to integrate into slimmer, more traditional-looking frames.
Bosch also says the new gearbox uses specially machined gears to make the motor virtually silent, while updated sensors and software provide smoother, more natural-feeling pedal assistance.
That’s particularly important for a motor like the Active Line Plus, where riders are often looking for an experience that feels like riding a regular bicycle, just with a bit of extra help.
The motor also supports Bosch’s eShift electronic shifting system, which can automatically manage gear changes for riders who prefer to focus on pedaling instead of shifting.
Bosch has additionally improved the motor’s sealing and bearings for better all-weather durability. The housing uses approximately 40% recycled aluminum, helping reduce the carbon footprint of its production.
Coming soon to new electric bikes
Trek will be the first North American bicycle brand to introduce the new Active Line Plus motor, installing it on the company’s Marlin+ electric bike.
Bosch also announced several other additions to its e-bike ecosystem, including a new compact LED Controller that’s 65% smaller than its predecessor, an updated ConnectModule with Bluetooth-based theft tracking, and a new 720 Wh PowerTube battery weighing just 8.6 lb (3.9 kg).
There’s also a new Intuvia 200 display, offering a 2.4-inch grayscale screen for riders who prefer a traditional handlebar-mounted display.
While high-performance e-bike motors tend to grab the headlines with increasingly outrageous torque figures, there’s something to be said for improvements to the more practical end of the market – something for the riders looking for convenient and effective transportation instead of peak performance figures.
For the average commuter or recreational rider, a quieter, lighter motor with plenty of usable power is likely to make a bigger difference than squeezing another few dozen Newton-meters out of an already powerful drive system.
And with Bosch’s extensive network of bicycle manufacturing partners, we can expect to see this updated motor making its way into plenty of new electric bikes.
